title: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer
summary: Defines a string syntax for identifying a specific value inside a JSON document, using slash-separated reference tokens that walk down through objects and arrays.

plainLanguage.summary: A JSON Pointer is a way of naming one value inside a JSON document, in the same way that a path names a file. It is a short string of steps, each one naming either a named field or a numbered item, and it can be written both inside a JSON string and inside a web address.

questions: how to reference a value in a json document
what does ~1 mean in json pointer
how to use json pointer in a url fragment
subtitle: A short string syntax for pointing at one specific value inside a JSON document.

tldr.problem: There was no standard way to name one particular value inside a JSON document, either in a JSON string or in a URI fragment identifier.
tldr.mechanism: A JSON Pointer is a string of zero or more reference tokens, each prefixed by '/'. Each token steps from the current value to an object member or an array element, starting at the document root.
tldr.outcome: The same pointer can be written as a JSON string or, with percent-encoding, as a URI fragment. What happens when a pointer fails to resolve is left to the application that uses it.

today: RFC 6901 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Applications that use it must still define how to handle pointers that do not resolve.

sections.title: What JSON Pointer Is
sections.content: This specification defines JSON Pointer, a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document. A JSON Pointer is meant to be easy to express both in a JSON string value and in a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) fragment identifier, so that the same pointer can travel inside a document or inside a web address.
sections.plainLanguage: One string syntax, two places to put it: inside the JSON itself, or after the number sign in a web address.

sections.title: Pointer Syntax
sections.content:
A JSON Pointer is a Unicode string containing a sequence of zero or more reference tokens, each prefixed by a '/' character. Because '~' and '/' have special meanings inside a pointer, a '~' in a token has to be written as '~0' and a '/' as '~1'.

The syntax in ABNF is:

json-pointer    = *( "/" reference-token )
reference-token = *( unescaped / escaped )
unescaped       = %x00-2E / %x30-7D / %x7F-10FFFF
   ; %x2F ('/') and %x7E ('~') are excluded from 'unescaped'
escaped         = "~" ( "0" / "1" )
  ; representing '~' and '/', respectively

A pointer that does not conform to this syntax is an error condition. The RFC also notes that JSON Pointers are specified in characters, not in bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: A pointer is a list of steps separated by slashes. Because the slash and the tilde are used by the syntax itself, they have to be escaped when they appear inside a name.

sections.title: Evaluating a Pointer
sections.content:
Evaluation starts at the root value of the document and ends at some value inside it. Each reference token is evaluated in turn.

Evaluation of a token begins by decoding the escaped character sequences. The order matters: '~1' is transformed to '/' first, and '~0' is transformed to '~' second. Doing it in that order avoids turning '~01' into '~1' and then into '/', which would be wrong, because '~01' should end up as '~1'.

If the value currently referenced is a JSON object, the new value is the member whose name the token names. The member name equals the token when it has the same number of Unicode characters and their code points match byte for byte, and no Unicode normalization is performed. If a member name is not unique in the object, the referenced member is undefined and evaluation fails.

If the value currently referenced is a JSON array, the token must contain either digits that represent an unsigned base-10 index, with no leading zero, so that the new value is the element at that zero-based index, or exactly the single character '-', which refers to the nonexistent member after the last element. The index syntax is array-index = %x30 / ( %x31-39 *(%x30-39) ).

An implementation evaluates each token against the document and raises an error if it cannot resolve a concrete value. Indexing an array with a non-numeric token is such an error, and so is using '-' to index an array, because it refers to an element that does not exist. Any error for which the application defines no specific action ends the evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: Start at the top of the document and walk down one step at a time. A step names a field of an object or a numbered item of an array, and if a step does not make sense the whole pointer fails.

sections.title: Pointers Inside JSON Strings
sections.content:
A JSON Pointer can be written as a JSON string value. All the quotation mark, reverse solidus and control characters must be escaped, as every JSON string requires. Before a JSON string is processed as a pointer, its backslash escape sequences must be unescaped.

The RFC's example document has a member with every awkward name: "foo": ["bar", "baz"], a member with an empty name, and members named "a/b", "c%d", "e^f", "g|h", "i\\j", "k\"l", " " and "m~n". The pointers that select them are "" for the whole document, "/foo" for the array, "/foo/0" for its first element, "/" for the member with the empty name, "/a~1b" for the member named a/b, and "/m~0n" for the member named m~n.
sections.plainLanguage: In a JSON string, a pointer with a slash in a name uses the tilde escape, and the JSON escaping of backslashes and quotes still applies on top of that.

sections.title: Pointers in URI Fragments
sections.content:
A JSON Pointer can also be written as a URI fragment identifier by encoding it into octets with UTF-8 and then percent-encoding the characters that the fragment rule of RFC 3986 does not allow. So the same document that "/c%d" selects in a JSON string is #/c%25d in a URI, and the space in a member name is #/%20.

The RFC is careful about one point: a media type has to name JSON Pointer as its fragment identifier syntax explicitly, usually in its registration. Just because a document is JSON does not mean that JSON Pointer can be used as its fragment identifier syntax, and in particular the fragment identifier syntax for application/json is not JSON Pointer.
sections.plainLanguage: In a web address the pointer is percent-encoded on top of the usual escaping. A media type has to opt in to this syntax before a pointer can be used after the number sign.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
When an error condition occurs, evaluation of the pointer fails to complete. Error conditions include invalid pointer syntax and a pointer that references a value that does not exist.

This specification does not define how errors are handled. An application of JSON Pointer should specify the impact and the handling of each kind of error. Some applications might stop processing at the first error, while others might recover from a missing value by inserting a default one.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says what counts as a failure but leaves the reaction to whoever uses pointers, because a database update and a web link want different things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A JSON Pointer is not guaranteed to reference a value that actually exists, so an application using pointers should define in advance how a pointer that does not resolve is handled.

The RFC also points out that a JSON pointer can contain the NUL character, so care is needed not to misinterpret that character in programming languages that use NUL to mark the end of a string.
sections.plainLanguage: A pointer may point at nothing, so the application has to say what to do about it. And a pointer can contain a null character, which can cut a string short in some languages.

data.title: JSON Pointer syntax
data.code:
json-pointer    = *( "/" reference-token )
reference-token = *( unescaped / escaped )
unescaped       = %x00-2E / %x30-7D / %x7F-10FFFF
escaped         = "~" ( "0" / "1" )

viz.caption: The rules that decide what a token means

items.title: Unescape in order
items.text: Turn ~1 into a slash first, then ~0 into a tilde, so that ~01 becomes ~1.

items.title: Object member
items.text: The token names the member, compared character by character with no normalization.

items.title: Array index
items.text: Digits without a leading zero, counting from zero.

items.title: The dash
items.text: A single dash names the position after the last element, which never exists.

items.title: Empty pointer
items.text: The empty string is the whole document.
